dietEvidence.body: The skull and blade-like serrated teeth are consistent with carnivory. No gut contents are known, and the prey species are not recorded.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A megalosaurid known from a partial skeleton from the Oxford Clay. The depositional setting is marine, but the animal was a terrestrial predator.
summary: A megalosaurid known from a partial skeleton from the Oxford Clay. The depositional setting is marine, but the animal was a terrestrial predator.

discovery.body: Named by Alick Walker in 1964 from the Middle Oxford Clay at Summertown, Oxford. The holotype, OUMNH J.13558, is a nearly complete but disarticulated skeleton discovered in 1871 and initially referred to Megalosaurus. It is the most complete Middle Jurassic theropod from Europe.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: A partial skeleton, mostly disarticulated, from a marine Clay.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Oxford Clay, Oxfordshire records the species in the Middle Jurassic. The numeric range used here is ≈165–161 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skeleton is moderately robust, with a large skull and strong forelimbs; the tail is long.

behaviour.body: Carnivory is inferred from the skull and blade-like teeth. The carcass was buried in marine Clay, but whether the animal lived near the coast or was washed in from inland is unknown.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from a partial skeleton, mostly disarticulated, from a marine Clay. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The species is known from a single, probably subadult skeleton from a marine Clay. The anatomy is well described, but adult size, integument and behaviour are not preserved. The marine setting complicates palaeoenvironmental interpretation.
